lessons.title: Where am I? (pwd)
lessons.concept: Before you can go anywhere, you need to know where you already are.

challenges.explanation:
pwd: Print Working Directory

Prints the full absolute path of your current location in the filesystem. Think of it like a "you are here" marker; it never moves you, it just reports where you already are.

No arguments needed. It always works from any location.

Syntax:  pwd
challenges.instruction: Your terminal just opened. You don't know where you are. Type pwd to find your current location.
challenges.hint: pwd takes no arguments. Just type: pwd
challenges.success_message: ✓ You're at /home/user, your home directory.

lessons.title: What's here? (ls)
lessons.concept: Knowing where you are is step one. Seeing what's there is step two.

challenges.explanation:
ls: List directory contents

Shows the files and folders inside a directory. Without any arguments it lists your current directory. On most systems:
  • directories appear in blue
  • regular files in white
  • executable files (.sh, .py) in green

Syntax:  ls [path]
challenges.instruction: You're in your home directory. See what files and folders are here.
challenges.hint: Just type ls with no arguments.
challenges.success_message: ✓ You can see your files and directories!

challenges.explanation:
ls with a path argument

You can pass any directory path to ls as an argument. This lets you look inside a directory without navigating into it first, useful for quickly checking contents before you decide to cd.

Syntax:  ls <directory>
Example: ls Downloads
challenges.instruction: List the contents of the Documents folder without entering it.
challenges.tip: 💡 Tip: press Tab to autocomplete directory names as you type.
challenges.hint: Pass the directory name as an argument: ls Documents
challenges.success_message: ✓ You can inspect any directory with ls, without moving into it!

lessons.title: Seeing more: ls flags
lessons.concept: Flags (options starting with -) modify how a command behaves. ls has many useful ones.

challenges.explanation:
The -l flag: long listing format

The -l flag (lowercase L) switches ls to "long format": one entry per line with full details:

  drwxr-xr-x  2  user  user  4096  Jan 14  Documents
  │           │   │     │     │     │        └─ name
  │           │   │     │     │     └─ last modified
  │           │   │     │     └─ size in bytes
  │           │   │     └─ group
  │           │   └─ owner
  │           └─ number of hard links
  └─ permissions (d=directory, r=read, w=write, x=execute)

Syntax:  ls -l [path]
challenges.instruction: See file details: permissions, size, and modification date. Use ls -l.
challenges.hint: -l stands for 'long listing format'.
challenges.success_message: ✓ Now you can see file sizes, permissions, and timestamps!

challenges.explanation:
The -a flag: show all files

By convention, any file whose name starts with a dot (.) is hidden; ls omits it by default. These "dotfiles" are typically:
  • shell config files: .bashrc, .zshrc
  • app config: .gitconfig, .vimrc
  • history files: .bash_history

The -a flag (all) makes them visible alongside regular files.

Syntax:  ls -a [path]
challenges.instruction: Some files start with a dot and are hidden. Reveal them all.
challenges.hint: The -a flag shows all files, including hidden ones (starting with .).
challenges.success_message: ✓ Hidden files often contain important configuration data!

challenges.explanation:
Combining flags: -la and ll

Flags can be combined in a single argument. -la (or equivalently -al) applies both -l and -a at once, giving you the full picture: every file, in long format.

Many Linux distributions also define ll as a shell alias for ls -la, so both are equivalent and very commonly used in practice.

Syntax:  ls -la   or   ls -al   or   ll
challenges.instruction: Combine both: show all files in long format. Try ls -la (or the shortcut ll).
challenges.hint: Combine flags: ls -la. Many systems also have 'll' as a shortcut.
challenges.success_message: ✓ Full picture: every file, every detail!

lessons.title: Moving around: cd
lessons.concept: Knowing what's in a directory is useful. Being able to move into it is essential.

challenges.explanation:
cd: Change Directory

Moves you into a different directory. After a successful cd, your shell prompt changes to reflect your new location.

You can use:
  • a relative path   cd Documents       (relative to where you are now)
  • an absolute path  cd /home/user/Documents  (works from anywhere)

If you try to cd into a file or a nonexistent path, you'll get an error; cd only works on directories.

Syntax:  cd <path>
challenges.instruction: Move into the Documents directory.
challenges.tip: 💡 Tip: type cd Doc and press Tab — the shell completes the rest.
challenges.hint: cd followed by a directory name moves you inside it: cd Documents
challenges.success_message: ✓ You're now inside Documents! Notice the prompt changed.

challenges.explanation:
Confirming your location with pwd

After navigating with cd, it's good practice to confirm you're where you expected. Your prompt shows a shortened version (~/Documents), but pwd always gives you the full absolute path with no ambiguity.

This challenge starts with you already inside Documents, as if you just completed the previous step.
challenges.instruction: Confirm your new location.
challenges.hint: You already know this one: pwd shows where you are.
challenges.success_message: ✓ /home/user/Documents, exactly where you expected!

challenges.explanation:
Navigating deeper, one step at a time

You can cd into a subdirectory by typing its name relative to your current position. Each cd takes you one level deeper into the directory tree.

You can also skip levels by chaining: cd projects/subdir, but one step at a time is often clearer when exploring an unfamiliar structure.

This challenge also starts inside Documents.
challenges.instruction: Go deeper: move into the projects subdirectory.
challenges.hint: You can keep navigating deeper with cd, one step at a time.
challenges.success_message: ✓ You're now at /home/user/Documents/projects!

lessons.title: Going back: cd ..
lessons.concept: Moving forward is easy. Knowing how to go back is just as important.

challenges.explanation:
cd ..: Go up one level

.. (two dots) is a special path name that always refers to the parent directory, the directory containing your current one. It works in any command, not just cd:
  ls ..          see what's in the parent directory
  cat ../notes.txt  read a file one level up

You start this challenge deep inside projects. Going up one level lands you in Documents.

Syntax:  cd ..
challenges.instruction: You start inside projects. Go back up one level to Documents.
challenges.hint: .. refers to the parent directory. cd .. moves you up one level.
challenges.success_message: ✓ Back in Documents!

challenges.explanation:
Going up again

Each cd .. moves you exactly one level up the tree. You can also go up multiple levels at once:
  cd ../..   goes up two levels
  cd ../../.. goes up three levels

This challenge starts where the previous one ended, in Documents. Going up from here takes you back to the home directory.

Syntax:  cd ..
challenges.instruction: Go up one more level to reach your home directory.
challenges.hint: Each cd .. goes up exactly one level in the directory tree.
challenges.success_message: ✓ Back home: /home/user!

lessons.title: Home shortcut: cd ~
lessons.concept: When you're deep in the tree, there's a faster way home than cd ../../..

challenges.explanation:
~: The home directory shortcut

~ (tilde) is a special symbol that always expands to your home directory (/home/user), regardless of where you are. You can use it in any path:
  ls ~/Documents         list your Documents from anywhere
  cd ~/Downloads         jump straight to Downloads
  cat ~/notes.txt        read a home file without moving

Running cd with no arguments at all is equivalent to cd ~; both take you straight home.

Syntax:  cd ~   or just   cd
challenges.instruction: You're deep inside the filesystem. Jump straight back home in one command.
challenges.hint: ~ is your home directory shortcut. Just 'cd' with no arguments also works.
challenges.success_message: ✓ Home in an instant, no matter how deep you were!

lessons.title: Absolute paths
lessons.concept: Relative paths depend on where you are. Absolute paths always work, from anywhere.

challenges.explanation:
Absolute paths: starting from /

Every location on a Linux filesystem can be described as an absolute path: one that starts from / (the root) and uniquely identifies a place regardless of your current directory.

Contrast:
  cd Documents         relative, only works if Documents is in your cwd
  cd /home/user/Documents  absolute, always works from anywhere

Absolute paths are especially useful in scripts, config files, or whenever you can't be sure where the user will be when the command runs.

Syntax:  cd /path/from/root
challenges.instruction: Navigate to /home/user/Downloads using its full absolute path.
challenges.hint: Absolute paths start with /. Type the full path: cd /home/user/Downloads
challenges.success_message: ✓ Absolute paths are reliable: they always work, no matter where you start!

challenges.explanation:
Listing after navigation

After landing somewhere new with cd, ls is the natural follow-up; it shows you what's there.

You can also combine both operations without moving:
  ls /home/user/Downloads  shows contents without changing your location

This challenge starts with you already in Downloads, as if you just ran the previous step.
challenges.instruction: List the contents of your new location.
challenges.hint: After cd, just type ls to see what's in your new directory.
challenges.success_message: ✓ You can see the files in Downloads!

lessons.title: Creating files (touch)
lessons.concept: Before you can write to a file, it needs to exist. touch creates it instantly.

challenges.explanation:
touch: Create an empty file

touch creates a new empty file if it doesn't already exist. If the file does exist, touch updates its "last modified" timestamp without changing its contents.

The name comes from the idea of "touching" a file to update its timestamp, but in practice it's mostly used to quickly create placeholder files.

Syntax:  touch <filename>
challenges.instruction: Create an empty file called memo.txt in your home directory.
challenges.hint: touch followed by the filename: touch memo.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ memo.txt created! Verify it with: ls

challenges.explanation:
touch with a path

You can pass a path to touch, not just a filename. This lets you create a file directly inside another directory without navigating there first.

Example:
  touch Documents/notes2.txt  creates notes2.txt inside Documents/

The parent directory must already exist; touch won't create directories for you.

Syntax:  touch <path/to/filename>
challenges.instruction: Create a file called log.txt inside the Documents directory.
challenges.hint: Use a relative path: touch Documents/log.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ log.txt created inside Documents/. You can create files anywhere with touch!

lessons.title: Creating directories (mkdir)
lessons.concept: Directories let you organise files into logical groups. mkdir creates them on demand.

challenges.explanation:
mkdir: Make Directory

Creates a new directory at the path you specify. The directory must not already exist, and the parent directory must be present.

After creating it, the directory is empty. You can then move files into it with mv, or create new files with touch.

Syntax:  mkdir <directory_name>
challenges.instruction: Create a new directory called Projects in your home directory.
challenges.hint: mkdir followed by the name: mkdir Projects
challenges.success_message: ✓ Projects/ created! Check it with: ls

challenges.explanation:
mkdir -p: Create nested directories

By default, mkdir fails if any part of the path doesn't exist:
  mkdir a/b/c   fails if a/ or a/b/ don't exist

The -p flag (parents) creates every missing directory along the path, all at once:
  mkdir -p a/b/c   creates a/, a/b/, and a/b/c/ in one step

This is extremely common in scripts and automation.

Syntax:  mkdir -p <nested/path>
challenges.instruction: Create the nested directory structure workspace/src — both directories at once.
challenges.hint: Use mkdir -p for nested directories: mkdir -p workspace/src
challenges.success_message: ✓ workspace/ and workspace/src/ created in one command!

lessons.title: Copying files (cp)
lessons.concept: cp duplicates a file. The original stays untouched; you get a fresh copy.

challenges.explanation:
cp: Copy

Creates an exact copy of a file at a new location. The source file is not affected.

Two forms:
  cp source dest_file   copies source to a new file called dest_file
  cp source dest_dir/   copies source into dest_dir, keeping the original name

Syntax:  cp <source> <destination>
challenges.instruction: Create a backup of notes.txt called notes_backup.txt.
challenges.hint: cp source destination: cp notes.txt notes_backup.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ notes_backup.txt created. notes.txt is untouched.

challenges.explanation:
cp to a different directory

When the destination is an existing directory, cp places the copy inside that directory under the same filename.

Example:
  cp report.txt /tmp/   creates /tmp/report.txt

You can also rename while moving:
  cp report.txt /tmp/backup_report.txt

Syntax:  cp <source> <destination_dir>/
challenges.instruction: Copy Documents/letter.txt into the Downloads directory.
challenges.hint: cp source destination_dir: cp Documents/letter.txt Downloads/
challenges.success_message: ✓ letter.txt now exists in both Documents/ and Downloads/!

lessons.title: Moving & renaming (mv)
lessons.concept: mv moves files between directories. When source and destination are in the same place, it's a rename.

challenges.explanation:
mv: Move (or rename)

mv moves a file from one location to another. Unlike cp, the original is removed.

When both source and destination are in the same directory, the file stays in place but gets a new name — this is how you rename files in Linux (there's no separate rename command).

Syntax:  mv <source> <destination>
challenges.instruction: Rename todo.txt to tasks.txt.
challenges.hint: mv old_name new_name: mv todo.txt tasks.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ todo.txt is now tasks.txt. mv is the standard way to rename files in Linux.

challenges.explanation:
mv to a different directory

When the destination is an existing directory, mv places the file inside it:
  mv notes.txt Documents/   moves notes.txt into Documents/

The original location no longer contains the file. You can verify with ls after the move.

You can also move and rename simultaneously:
  mv notes.txt Documents/my_notes.txt

Syntax:  mv <source> <destination_dir>/
challenges.instruction: Move notes.txt into the Documents directory.
challenges.hint: mv source destination_dir: mv notes.txt Documents/
challenges.success_message: ✓ notes.txt is now inside Documents/. It no longer exists in the home directory.

lessons.title: Removing files (rm)
lessons.concept: rm permanently deletes files. There is no Recycle Bin — what's deleted is gone.

challenges.explanation:
rm: Remove

Deletes files permanently. There is no undo, no trash. Once you rm a file, it's gone.

Always double-check what you're deleting before pressing Enter. For safety, avoid wildcards like rm * until you're very comfortable with the tool.

Syntax:  rm <filename>
challenges.instruction: Remove temp.txt from your home directory.
challenges.hint: rm followed by the filename: rm temp.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ temp.txt deleted. Remember: rm is permanent — no recycle bin!

challenges.explanation:
rm with a path

You can remove a file in any directory by providing its path, relative or absolute.

Example:
  rm Downloads/archive.zip
  rm /tmp/old_file.txt

For directories, rm needs the -r flag (recursive) to delete the directory and everything inside it. Never run rm -rf on an important directory — it deletes everything immediately.

Syntax:  rm <path/to/file>
challenges.instruction: Remove the archive file from the Downloads directory.
challenges.hint: Provide the path: rm Downloads/archive.zip
challenges.success_message: ✓ archive.zip removed from Downloads/!

lessons.title: Removing directories (rmdir)
lessons.concept: rmdir removes a directory — but only if it's completely empty.

challenges.explanation:
rmdir: Remove Directory

Removes an empty directory. If the directory contains any files or subdirectories, rmdir will refuse with an error.

This safety feature means rmdir can never accidentally delete your data. For removing a directory with contents, you would use rm -r (which is much more dangerous).

Syntax:  rmdir <directory>
challenges.instruction: Remove the empty directory called tmp.
challenges.hint: rmdir followed by the directory name: rmdir tmp
challenges.success_message: ✓ tmp/ removed. rmdir only works when the directory is empty — that's by design!

challenges.explanation:
rmdir on another empty directory

You can use rmdir with any path to an empty directory, not just names in the current folder.

If you try to rmdir a directory that still has files, you'll get:
  rmdir: failed to remove 'dir': Directory not empty

In that case, you'd need to empty the directory first (or use rm -r, carefully).

Syntax:  rmdir <path/to/directory>
challenges.instruction: Remove the other empty directory called old.
challenges.hint: rmdir old
challenges.success_message: ✓ Both empty directories cleaned up. Use ls to confirm they're gone.

lessons.title: Displaying files (cat)
lessons.concept: cat reads a file and prints every line to the terminal. Short for 'concatenate'.

challenges.explanation:
cat: Concatenate and print

Displays the entire contents of a file, line by line. It's the quickest way to read a short text file without opening an editor.

The name comes from its original purpose: concatenating (joining) multiple files. But reading single files is its most common everyday use.

Syntax:  cat <filename>
challenges.instruction: Display the contents of notes.txt.
challenges.hint: cat followed by the filename: cat notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ You can read any text file with cat!

challenges.explanation:
cat with a path

You can cat any file by providing its path, not just files in your current directory.

Example:
  cat Documents/letter.txt
  cat /etc/hosts

cat dumps the whole file at once. For large files, use head or tail instead to preview just part of the content.

Syntax:  cat <path/to/file>
challenges.instruction: Display the letter inside your Documents folder.
challenges.hint: Provide the path: cat Documents/letter.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ cat works with any path, not just files in the current directory.

lessons.title: Printing text (echo)
lessons.concept: echo prints whatever you give it. It's fundamental to scripting, messaging, and debugging.

challenges.explanation:
echo: Print a line of text

Outputs its arguments to the terminal, followed by a newline. Arguments are separated by spaces; echo prints them with a single space between each.

Common uses:
  • print a message  echo Done!
  • check a variable  echo $HOME  (shows /home/user)
  • write to a file   echo text > file.txt  (redirection, covered later)

Syntax:  echo <text>
challenges.instruction: Print the message: Hello Linux
challenges.hint: echo followed by the text: echo Hello Linux
challenges.success_message: ✓ echo prints its arguments to the terminal.

challenges.explanation:
echo with multiple words

echo accepts as many words as you give it and joins them with spaces in the output.

  echo one two three   →  one two three

This becomes powerful in scripts: you can use echo to print status messages, labels, and debug info, and combine it with redirection (>) to write text to files without an editor.

Syntax:  echo <word1> <word2> ...
challenges.instruction: Use echo to print: Hello user
challenges.hint: echo Hello user
challenges.success_message: ✓ echo outputs exactly what you give it!

lessons.title: First lines (head)
lessons.concept: head shows the beginning of a file — essential when files are too large to cat.

challenges.explanation:
head: Output the first N lines

By default, head shows the first 10 lines of a file. Use -n to specify a different number.

This is invaluable when dealing with large log files or data exports: instead of flooding your terminal with thousands of lines, you peek at the structure first.

Syntax:  head -n <count> <filename>
challenges.instruction: Show the first 3 lines of Documents/letter.txt.
challenges.hint: head -n 3 Documents/letter.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ head shows the top of any file without loading it all!

challenges.explanation:
head on different files

head works on any readable text file. You can combine it with a path just like cat.

Useful pattern:
  head -n 1 file.txt  shows only the very first line (great for CSV headers)
  head -n 5 log.txt   peek at the first 5 log entries

Syntax:  head -n <count> <path/to/file>
challenges.instruction: Show the first 2 lines of notes.txt.
challenges.hint: head -n 2 notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ head -n N shows exactly N lines from the top of any file.

lessons.title: Last lines (tail)
lessons.concept: tail shows the end of a file — especially useful for log files where new entries appear at the bottom.

challenges.explanation:
tail: Output the last N lines

Mirror of head: shows the last N lines of a file instead of the first. Default is 10 lines without -n.

Log files grow downward (newest entries at the bottom), making tail the go-to tool for checking what just happened:
  tail -n 20 /var/log/syslog   last 20 system events

Syntax:  tail -n <count> <filename>
challenges.instruction: Show the last 2 lines of notes.txt.
challenges.hint: tail -n 2 notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ tail reads from the bottom up — great for log files!

challenges.explanation:
tail with a path

Like head and cat, tail accepts any path to a readable file.

Pro tip: tail -f file.txt follows a file in real time, printing new lines as they're added. This is the standard way to monitor a live log file. The -f variant isn't covered in this lesson, but it's worth knowing about.

Syntax:  tail -n <count> <path/to/file>
challenges.instruction: Show the last 3 lines of Documents/letter.txt.
challenges.hint: tail -n 3 Documents/letter.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ tail -n 3 shows the last 3 lines of any file. You've now mastered head and tail!

lessons.title: Searching text (grep)
lessons.concept: grep scans a file line by line and prints only the lines that match a pattern.

challenges.explanation:
grep: Global Regular Expression Print

Searches a file for lines matching a pattern and prints each matching line. The pattern is case-sensitive by default.

Syntax:  grep <pattern> <file>

Examples:
  grep error log.txt        lines containing 'error'
  grep root /etc/passwd     lines mentioning 'root'

grep exits with code 0 if it found matches, 1 if not — useful in scripts.
challenges.instruction: Find all lines in notes.txt that contain the word TODO.
challenges.hint: grep pattern file: grep TODO notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ grep found every line containing TODO!

challenges.explanation:
grep -i: Case-insensitive search

By default, grep is case-sensitive: 'Meeting' and 'meeting' are different.

The -i flag (ignore case) makes the search match regardless of uppercase or lowercase:
  grep -i meeting notes.txt  matches 'Meeting', 'MEETING', 'meeting'

Use -i when you're not sure how the text was typed, or when searching user-generated content.

Syntax:  grep -i <pattern> <file>
challenges.instruction: Search for lines containing 'meeting' in notes.txt, ignoring case.
challenges.hint: Add -i for case-insensitive: grep -i meeting notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ -i makes grep ignore case — it matched 'Meeting' even though you searched for 'meeting'!

challenges.explanation:
grep -n: Show line numbers

The -n flag adds the line number before each matching line:
  grep -n pattern file
  Output: 3:matching line content

Line numbers are useful when you want to jump to a specific location in an editor, or when scanning a script for where something happens.

Syntax:  grep -n <pattern> <file>
challenges.instruction: Find lines containing 'Alice' in Documents/scores.csv and show the line numbers.
challenges.hint: Add -n to show line numbers: grep -n Alice Documents/scores.csv
challenges.success_message: ✓ grep -n shows exactly which line number each match is on!

lessons.title: Finding files (find)
lessons.concept: find searches the filesystem for files and directories matching your criteria.

challenges.explanation:
find: Search for files

Searches a directory tree for entries that match criteria you specify. Unlike ls, find descends into all subdirectories automatically.

Basic form:
  find <start_dir> [options]

To find a specific file by name:
  find . -name notes.txt   searches from . (current dir) downward

The dot (.) means "start here". Results are printed as paths relative to the start.

Syntax:  find <path> -name <filename>
challenges.instruction: Find the file notes.txt starting from your current directory.
challenges.hint: find . -name notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ find searches all subdirectories recursively!

challenges.explanation:
find -type d: Find directories

The -type flag filters by entry type:
  -type f   regular files only
  -type d   directories only

This is useful when you want to list all directories in a project, or find all files without directories cluttering the output.

Syntax:  find <path> -type d
challenges.instruction: List all directories under your current location.
challenges.hint: Use -type d to find directories: find . -type d
challenges.success_message: ✓ find . -type d lists every directory in the tree!

challenges.explanation:
find in a specific subdirectory

You don't have to start find from . every time. You can give it any directory as the starting point to narrow the search:
  find Documents -name letter.txt   only searches inside Documents/

This is much faster on large filesystems when you know roughly where the file lives.

Syntax:  find <specific_dir> -name <filename>
challenges.instruction: Find the file letter.txt, but search only inside the Documents directory.
challenges.hint: Replace . with the directory to search: find Documents -name letter.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ Limiting find to a subdirectory keeps results focused and searches faster!

lessons.title: Counting (wc)
lessons.concept: wc counts lines, words, and bytes in a file — quick stats without opening it.

challenges.explanation:
wc: Word Count

Without flags, wc prints three numbers: lines, words, and bytes. You almost always want just one at a time:
  -l   count lines only
  -w   count words only
  -c   count bytes only

Line counting (-l) is especially useful: how many entries in this log? How many rows in this CSV?

Syntax:  wc -l <file>   (or -w, -c)
challenges.instruction: Count the number of lines in notes.txt.
challenges.hint: wc -l counts lines: wc -l notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ wc -l is one of the most common one-liners in shell scripting!

challenges.explanation:
wc -w: Count words

A 'word' for wc is any sequence of characters separated by whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines).

This is useful for rough word counts in text files, or for counting tokens in a list where each item is on its own line.

Syntax:  wc -w <file>
challenges.instruction: Count the number of words in todo.txt.
challenges.hint: wc -w counts words: wc -w todo.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ wc -w counted all the words in your to-do list!

lessons.title: Sorting lines (sort)
lessons.concept: sort reads a file's lines and outputs them in order. Alphabetical by default.

challenges.explanation:
sort: Sort lines of text

Reads a file and prints its lines in alphabetical (lexicographic) order. The original file is unchanged; output goes to the terminal.

Flags:
  sort file.txt   alphabetical (A–Z)
  sort -r file.txt  reverse (Z–A)
  sort -n file.txt  numeric order (1, 2, 10 instead of 1, 10, 2)
  sort -u file.txt  unique: removes duplicate lines

Syntax:  sort [flags] <file>
challenges.instruction: Sort the lines of todo.txt alphabetically.
challenges.hint: sort followed by the filename: sort todo.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ sort reorganises the lines alphabetically!

challenges.explanation:
sort -r: Reverse order

The -r flag reverses the sort direction: Z before A, or (with -n) largest numbers first.

Reverse sort is often used for:
  • showing the largest files first (du output)
  • showing the most recent entries first (when dates are formatted as YYYY-MM-DD)
  • finding the last item alphabetically in a list

Syntax:  sort -r <file>
challenges.instruction: Sort todo.txt in reverse alphabetical order.
challenges.hint: Add -r for reverse order: sort -r todo.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ sort -r inverts the order — last becomes first!

lessons.title: Removing duplicates (uniq)
lessons.concept: uniq filters out adjacent duplicate lines. Often used after sort to deduplicate a list.

challenges.explanation:
uniq: Filter adjacent duplicates

uniq removes consecutive duplicate lines from its input. The key word is adjacent: it only removes repeats that are next to each other. Non-adjacent duplicates are not removed.

This is why uniq is almost always paired with sort first:
  sort list.txt | uniq   (pipes covered in a later section)

For now, the file Documents/duplicates.txt already has adjacent duplicates for you to practice with.

Syntax:  uniq <file>
challenges.instruction: Remove adjacent duplicate lines from Documents/duplicates.txt.
challenges.hint: uniq followed by the filename: uniq Documents/duplicates.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ uniq collapsed consecutive duplicates into single lines!

challenges.explanation:
uniq -c: Count occurrences

The -c flag prepends each output line with the number of times it appeared consecutively:
  2 apple    (appeared 2 times in a row)
  1 banana   (appeared once)
  3 cherry   (appeared 3 times in a row)

This is a fast way to find the most repeated items in a sorted list.

Syntax:  uniq -c <file>
challenges.instruction: Show each unique line in Documents/duplicates.txt along with how many times it appeared.
challenges.hint: Add -c to count: uniq -c Documents/duplicates.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ uniq -c shows the count for each group of duplicates!

lessons.title: Extracting columns (cut)
lessons.concept: cut slices out columns from structured text — great for CSV and tabular data.

challenges.explanation:
cut: Extract fields from lines

cut selects specific columns (fields) from each line. For delimited files like CSVs:
  -d ,   use comma as the delimiter
  -f 1   extract field number 1 (first column)

The file Documents/scores.csv has three columns: name, score, grade.

Syntax:  cut -d <delimiter> -f <field_number> <file>
challenges.instruction: Extract the first column (names) from Documents/scores.csv.
challenges.hint: cut -d , -f 1 Documents/scores.csv
challenges.success_message: ✓ cut extracted just the names column from the CSV!

challenges.explanation:
cut with a different field number

Change -f to extract any column you want:
  -f 1   first column
  -f 2   second column
  -f 3   third column
  -f 1,3   first AND third columns

cut is especially powerful when combined with sort and other tools via pipes (covered later).

Syntax:  cut -d <delimiter> -f <field_number> <file>
challenges.instruction: Extract the second column (scores) from Documents/scores.csv.
challenges.hint: Change -f to 2: cut -d , -f 2 Documents/scores.csv
challenges.success_message: ✓ cut -f 2 extracted the scores column. You can pull any column from structured text!

lessons.title: File metadata (stat)
lessons.concept: stat shows everything about a file: size, permissions, timestamps, inode number.

challenges.explanation:
stat: Display file status

shows detailed metadata about a file or directory:
  • File name and path
  • Size in bytes
  • Block size and blocks used
  • File type and permissions
  • Inode number (filesystem identifier)
  • Number of hard links
  • Owner (UID) and group (GID)
  • Access, Modify, and Change timestamps

ls -l shows a subset of this; stat shows everything.

Syntax:  stat <file>
challenges.instruction: Show full metadata for notes.txt.
challenges.hint: stat followed by the filename: stat notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ stat reveals every detail stored about a file in the filesystem!

challenges.explanation:
stat on executables and scripts

stat is especially useful for executable files, where you want to confirm:
  • permissions (is it actually executable?)
  • who owns it
  • when it was last modified

The Downloads directory contains a shell script, setup.sh. Let's inspect it.

Syntax:  stat <path/to/file>
challenges.instruction: Show the metadata for Downloads/setup.sh.
challenges.hint: stat Downloads/setup.sh
challenges.success_message: ✓ stat on a script shows its permissions, owner, and last modification time.

lessons.title: File types (file)
lessons.concept: file identifies what a file actually contains — regardless of its extension.

challenges.explanation:
file: Determine file type

Reads the content of a file and reports what type it is. Unlike the file extension (which can be wrong or missing), file inspects the actual data (magic bytes) to determine the type.

Examples of output:
  ASCII text
  Zip archive data
  PDF document
  JPEG image data
  Bourne-Again shell script

Syntax:  file <filename>
challenges.instruction: Determine the type of Downloads/archive.zip.
challenges.hint: file followed by the path: file Downloads/archive.zip
challenges.success_message: ✓ file identified the archive type from its content, not just its name!

challenges.explanation:
file on different formats

file helps when:
  • a file has no extension and you don't know what it is
  • an extension looks wrong (someone named a shell script as .txt)
  • you want to confirm a download is what it claims to be

Let's inspect the PDF in your Documents folder.

Syntax:  file <path/to/file>
challenges.instruction: Determine the file type of Documents/report.pdf.
challenges.hint: file Documents/report.pdf
challenges.success_message: ✓ file reads the file content to identify its true type!

lessons.title: Changing permissions (chmod)
lessons.concept: chmod controls who can read, write, and execute a file.

challenges.explanation:
chmod: Change file mode (permissions)

Linux permissions have three categories:
  u (user/owner)   g (group)   o (others)

And three permission bits per category:
  r (read=4)   w (write=2)   x (execute=1)

Symbolic form:
  chmod +x file   add execute for everyone
  chmod -w file   remove write for everyone
  chmod u+x file  add execute for owner only

Octal form (sum r+w+x per category):
  chmod 755 file  → rwxr-xr-x
  chmod 644 file  → rw-r--r--

Syntax:  chmod <mode> <file>
challenges.instruction: Make Downloads/setup.sh executable for everyone (add +x).
challenges.hint: chmod +x adds execute permission: chmod +x Downloads/setup.sh
challenges.success_message: ✓ setup.sh is now executable! Verify with: stat Downloads/setup.sh

challenges.explanation:
chmod with octal notation

Octal notation sets all permissions at once using three digits (owner, group, others):
  6 = rw-  (read + write)
  4 = r--  (read only)
  7 = rwx  (read + write + execute)
  5 = r-x  (read + execute)

Common patterns:
  644  regular files     (owner rw, others r)
  755  executables/dirs  (owner rwx, others rx)
  600  private files     (owner rw only)

Syntax:  chmod <octal> <file>
challenges.instruction: Set notes.txt to standard file permissions: rw-r--r-- (octal 644).
challenges.hint: Use octal notation: chmod 644 notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ 644 is the standard permission for regular text files: owner can edit, everyone else can read.

lessons.title: Changing ownership (chown)
lessons.concept: chown changes who owns a file. Usually requires root on real systems.

challenges.explanation:
chown: Change owner

Every file has an owner (a user) and a group. chown changes one or both:
  chown alice file       changes owner to alice
  chown alice:devs file  changes owner to alice and group to devs
  chown :devs file       changes only the group

On a real Linux system, changing ownership typically requires root (sudo chown ...) unless you're giving away a file you own.

In this simulator you can practice the syntax freely.

Syntax:  chown <owner> <file>   or   chown <owner>:<group> <file>
challenges.instruction: Change the owner of notes.txt to root.
challenges.hint: chown new_owner filename: chown root notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ notes.txt owner changed to root. Check it with: stat notes.txt

challenges.explanation:
chown with owner and group

The colon syntax lets you set both owner and group in one command:
  chown user:users file   sets owner=user, group=users

Groups are used to share files with a team:
  • files owned by group 'devs' can be read/written by all members of devs
  • combined with chmod g+rw, the whole group gets write access

Syntax:  chown <owner>:<group> <file>
challenges.instruction: Change the owner to user and the group to users on notes.txt.
challenges.hint: Use the colon syntax: chown user:users notes.txt
challenges.success_message: ✓ Owner set to user, group set to users. The owner:group pattern is very common in team setups.

lessons.title: Disk usage (du)
lessons.concept: du shows how much disk space a file or directory is using.

challenges.explanation:
du: Disk Usage

Reports the disk space used by files and directories. Without flags it prints sizes in 512-byte blocks, which is hard to read.

The -h flag (human-readable) converts sizes to KB, MB, GB:
  du -h Documents   shows size of each item in Documents/

du descends into subdirectories by default, showing each one.

Syntax:  du -h <path>
challenges.instruction: Show the disk usage of the Documents directory in human-readable format.
challenges.hint: du -h for human-readable sizes: du -h Documents
challenges.success_message: ✓ du -h shows how much space each directory and file occupies!

challenges.explanation:
du -sh: Summary only

The -s flag (summary) suppresses subdirectory listing and shows only the total for the given path:
  du -h .    shows every file/dir under current directory
  du -sh .   shows only the grand total

Combining -s and -h gives a quick answer to 'how big is this directory?'

Syntax:  du -sh <path>
challenges.instruction: Show the total size of your entire home directory (current directory) as a single summary.
challenges.hint: Combine -s and -h: du -sh .
challenges.success_message: ✓ du -sh gives you the total in one line — great for a quick size check!

lessons.title: Disk free (df)
lessons.concept: df shows total, used, and available space for each mounted filesystem.

challenges.explanation:
df: Disk Free

Reports the amount of disk space available on each filesystem (mounted partition or device).

Without flags, sizes are in 1KB blocks. Each row shows:
  Filesystem   Size   Used   Available   Use%   Mounted on

df answers 'is the disk almost full?' at a glance.

Syntax:  df
challenges.instruction: Check the available disk space on your system.
challenges.hint: df takes no required arguments: just type df
challenges.success_message: ✓ df gives you a snapshot of disk usage across all filesystems!

challenges.explanation:
df -h: Human-readable output

Like du, the -h flag makes df output human-readable sizes (MB, GB) instead of raw blocks:
  df -h   much easier to interpret

This is almost always what you want. On a real server, 'df -h' is one of the first commands a sysadmin runs when investigating disk issues.

Syntax:  df -h
challenges.instruction: Show disk space in human-readable format.
challenges.hint: Add -h for human-readable: df -h
challenges.success_message: ✓ df -h is the standard disk space check — easy to read at a glance.

lessons.title: Who are you? (whoami & id)
lessons.concept: whoami and id tell you who you are in the system — essential in multi-user environments.

challenges.explanation:
whoami: Print current username

Outputs the username of the currently logged-in user. Simple, fast, and surprisingly useful:
  • confirms which account you're running as
  • critical in scripts to verify you're not accidentally running as root
  • verifies that sudo su or su commands worked

No arguments needed.

Syntax:  whoami
challenges.instruction: Find out which user you are currently logged in as.
challenges.hint: Just type: whoami
challenges.success_message: ✓ You're logged in as 'user'. Always good to confirm!

challenges.explanation:
id: Full user and group information

id gives more detail than whoami:
  uid=1000(user)         your numeric user ID and username
  gid=1000(user)         your primary group ID and name
  groups=1000(user),...  all groups you belong to

Group membership controls what files you can access. For example:
  group 'sudo'  means you can run sudo
  group 'adm'   means you can read system logs

Syntax:  id
challenges.instruction: Show your full user ID, group ID, and all group memberships.
challenges.hint: Just type: id
challenges.success_message: ✓ id shows your UID, GID, and all group memberships — more detail than whoami!

lessons.title: System name (hostname & uname)
lessons.concept: hostname shows the machine's network name; uname shows the operating system details.

challenges.explanation:
hostname: Show the machine name

Prints the hostname of the current machine — the name it uses on the network. In server environments you SSH into multiple machines; hostname reminds you which one you're on.

It's also used in scripts to make behavior conditional on which host is running them:
  if [ "$(hostname)" = "webserver" ]; then ...

Syntax:  hostname
challenges.instruction: Check the hostname of this machine.
challenges.hint: Just type: hostname
challenges.success_message: ✓ This machine's hostname is 'linux-quest'!

challenges.explanation:
uname: Print system information

uname (unix name) reports information about the operating system and kernel.

Flags:
  uname      print kernel name only (e.g. Linux)
  uname -s   same as uname alone
  uname -n   hostname
  uname -r   kernel release (version number)
  uname -m   machine hardware (x86_64, arm64)
  uname -a   all of the above at once

Syntax:  uname [-a]
challenges.instruction: Print all system information at once with uname -a.
challenges.hint: uname -a shows all system info: uname -a
challenges.success_message: ✓ uname -a shows kernel, hostname, version, and architecture in one line!

lessons.title: Date & time (date)
lessons.concept: date prints the current date and time. In scripts it's used to timestamp files and logs.

challenges.explanation:
date: Print current date and time

Outputs the current date and time in a human-readable format:
  Tue Jan 16 09:05:00 UTC 2024

date has a rich formatting system: you can produce any date format with + and format codes:
  date +%Y-%m-%d         2024-01-16
  date +%H:%M            09:05
  date +%s               Unix timestamp (seconds since 1970)

In scripts, date is often used to create unique filenames: backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz

Syntax:  date
challenges.instruction: Show the current date and time.
challenges.hint: Just type: date
challenges.success_message: ✓ date gives you the current system time — useful for timestamping and logging!

challenges.explanation:
uname -s: Kernel name only

You've already seen uname -a (all info). Sometimes you only want one piece, like just the kernel name:
  uname -s   Linux

This is more useful in scripts than in interactive use:
  OS=$(uname -s)
  if [ "$OS" = "Linux" ]; then
    # Linux-specific steps
  fi

Compare this to uname -a which dumps everything at once.

Syntax:  uname -s
challenges.instruction: Print only the kernel name (operating system type).
challenges.hint: uname -s prints just the kernel name: uname -s
challenges.success_message: ✓ uname -s confirms the OS type. On this machine it's Linux!

lessons.title: Running processes (ps)
lessons.concept: ps lists the processes currently running on the system.

challenges.explanation:
ps: Process Status

Displays a snapshot of current running processes. By default it shows only the processes belonging to your current terminal session:
  PID   process ID (unique number)
  TTY   terminal the process is attached to
  TIME  CPU time consumed
  CMD   command name

Every running program has a PID. You use PIDs to send signals (kill, pause, etc.) to processes.

Syntax:  ps
challenges.instruction: List the processes in your current terminal session.
challenges.hint: Just type: ps
challenges.success_message: ✓ ps shows the processes attached to your session!

challenges.explanation:
ps aux: All processes

To see every process on the whole system, use the aux flags:
  a   show processes from all users
  u   user-oriented format (shows username, CPU%, MEM%)
  x   include processes not attached to a terminal

The output includes system daemons, web servers, databases — everything running.

On a busy server, ps aux | grep nginx (covered with pipes later) is how you check if a service is running.

Syntax:  ps aux
challenges.instruction: List all processes running on the system.
challenges.hint: ps aux shows all processes: ps aux
challenges.success_message: ✓ ps aux reveals every running process on the system!

lessons.title: Environment variables (env & printenv)
lessons.concept: Environment variables are key-value pairs that configure the shell and programs.

challenges.explanation:
env: Print environment variables

Environment variables store configuration that programs inherit automatically:
  HOME     your home directory
  PATH     directories searched for commands
  USER     your username
  SHELL    the current shell
  EDITOR   your default text editor
  LANG     language and locale settings

env with no arguments prints all of them. Programs like Python, Node, and nginx read these to configure themselves.

Syntax:  env
challenges.instruction: Print all current environment variables.
challenges.hint: Just type: env
challenges.success_message: ✓ env reveals all the environment variables available to your shell and programs!

challenges.explanation:
printenv: Another way to view env vars

printenv is an alias for env in many contexts. Both print the same environment variables.

In practice:
  env          full list of variables
  printenv     same full list
  printenv HOME  print just the HOME variable

You'll see both in the wild. Knowing they're interchangeable saves confusion.

Syntax:  printenv
challenges.instruction: Print all environment variables using printenv.
challenges.hint: Just type: printenv
challenges.success_message: ✓ printenv and env are interchangeable for listing all variables!

lessons.title: Command history (history)
lessons.concept: history shows every command you've run. Never type a long command twice.

challenges.explanation:
history: Show command history

Prints a numbered list of the commands you've run in the current session. Each entry shows the command number and the command itself:
  1  ls
  2  cd Documents
  3  cat notes.txt

The number lets you re-run a command without retyping it:
  !3   re-runs command 3
  !!   re-runs the last command

This is invaluable when you've typed a long command and want to repeat it.

Syntax:  history
challenges.instruction: View your command history for this session.
challenges.hint: Just type: history
challenges.success_message: ✓ history shows every command you've run — all your steps are recorded!

challenges.explanation:
History grows as you work

Every command you type gets added to the history list. If you run history again now, you'll see the previous history call itself has been added.

In the real bash shell, history persists across sessions (stored in ~/.bash_history). The file already exists in your home directory and contains some earlier commands from a simulated session.

You can also search history with Ctrl+R in a real terminal: press Ctrl+R, start typing, and bash finds the most recent matching command.

Syntax:  history
challenges.instruction: Run history again to see the list has grown with your recent commands.
challenges.hint: Type history again — you'll see it in the list itself now!
challenges.success_message: ✓ Every command adds to history. The longer you work, the more useful history becomes!

lessons.title: Locating commands (which)
lessons.concept: which tells you exactly where a command lives on the filesystem.

challenges.explanation:
which: Locate a command

Searches directories in your PATH for the executable that runs when you type a command name. Prints the full path of the first match found.

Useful for:
  • confirming which version of a tool you're running
  • debugging PATH issues (wrong version being used)
  • checking if a program is installed at all

If the command isn't found in PATH, which prints nothing and returns exit code 1.

Syntax:  which <command>
challenges.instruction: Find out where the ls command is located.
challenges.hint: which followed by the command name: which ls
challenges.success_message: ✓ which showed you the full path to ls — that's the file that runs when you type ls!

challenges.explanation:
which on other commands

which works on any command in your PATH:
  which python    /usr/bin/python
  which git       /usr/bin/git
  which bash      /bin/bash

If you have multiple versions installed (like python2 and python3), which shows the first one found in PATH, which may not be what you expect. That's when it becomes a debugging tool.

Syntax:  which <command>
challenges.instruction: Find out where the grep command is installed.
challenges.hint: which grep
challenges.success_message: ✓ which grep shows the full path to the grep executable on this system!

lessons.title: Reading manuals (man)
lessons.concept: man opens the built-in manual for any command. The answer is always in the manual.

challenges.explanation:
man: Manual pages

Every standard Linux command has a built-in manual page. man opens it:
  man ls     the full documentation for ls
  man grep   everything grep can do
  man man    the manual for man itself

Manual pages follow a standard structure:
  NAME        command name and one-line description
  SYNOPSIS    usage syntax
  DESCRIPTION full explanation
  OPTIONS     all flags and what they do
  EXAMPLES    common usage patterns
  SEE ALSO    related commands

In this simulator, man shows a condensed summary.

Syntax:  man <command>
challenges.instruction: Open the manual page for the ls command.
challenges.hint: man followed by the command name: man ls
challenges.success_message: ✓ man ls shows you everything ls can do — flags you didn't know about!

challenges.explanation:
man on other commands

Make it a habit: when you encounter an unfamiliar flag or want to know all options for a command, reach for man first.

In a real terminal, man opens in a pager (usually less). You navigate with:
  space / Page Down  scroll down
  b / Page Up        scroll up
  /pattern           search forward
  q                  quit

This simulator shows the summary inline.

Syntax:  man <command>
challenges.instruction: Read the manual page for grep.
challenges.hint: man grep
challenges.success_message: ✓ Congratulations! You've completed all lessons. You now know your way around a Linux terminal!
